title: A check: audited federal money from the City against everything the City ledger paid
question: Does any organization’s audit show more federal money from the City than the City’s ledger shows it paying the organization in total?
finding: Almost none. In 444 audited organization-years with federal money from the City, 4 at 2 organizations show more in the audit than the whole of the City’s payments for the same months, by $100,000 and a tenth or more: The Yerba Buena Gardens Conservancy (year ended 2025-06-30: $11.2 million audited, $7.8 million paid); Main Street Launch (year ended 2025-06-30: $1.8 million audited, $282,601 paid); The Yerba Buena Gardens Conservancy (year ended 2021-06-30: $6.9 million audited, $5.7 million paid); Main Street Launch (year ended 2022-06-30: $1.5 million audited, $1.1 million paid). In the rest the audited figure fits inside the ledger.
how: Each audit’s total of awards whose pass-through body is the City, loans left out, against the payment-table total for the same employer number spread onto the audit period by days.
limits: A difference here usually has an ordinary cause: the ledger files a payment under a later fiscal-year label than the year it was earned; a revolving loan fund, or income from land bought with federal money and counted as federal programme income, is spent by the organization without a City payment in that year; the City pays an affiliate or a payee spelling not tied to the employer number. Each row needs the grant agreement before anything is read into it. For the fiscal years covered here, the federal audit threshold depends on the start of the entity’s fiscal year. It was $750,000 in federal awards expended across all programs for years starting before October 1, 2024, and $1 million for years starting on or after that date. An entity reaches the threshold at either amount. City payments alone cannot establish how much federal funding the recipient expended.
